body:
On examining the code, there's a check in the canvas item code for whether physics interpolation is enabled, but also for whether the object is visible:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/1aaf20b1f1f3ab59f04db74b166540327a3f1f90/scene/main/canvas_item.cpp#L378-L382

This unfortunately means that the reset workaround will fail for objects that are initially invisible. I'm assuming that this is done for performance reasons, but it seems like there's currently no way for the user to override that and force a reset of all nodes regardless of their current status.

Updated minimum reproduction showing where the workaround fails:
[PhysicsLerpIssueV2.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18325744/PhysicsLerpIssueV2.zip)

To reproduce:
- Uncheck "Make Visible"
- Check "Enable Workaround"
- Enable Physics Lerp
- Disable Physics Lerp
- Uncheck "Enable Workaround"
- Check "Make Visible"
- Enable Physics Lerp

Generally switching the global on / off isn't well supported intentionally, and the `set_physics_interpolation_mode()` as these aren't primarily intended to be used at runtime (except for debugging). The idea is generally that you would build your scenes in the editor and set their interpolation modes etc (physics interpolation is always off in the editor).

So getting that to be seamless at runtime is more of a feature request, and would need a use case, but it can probably be done simply with a reset on the root node as you are doing.

In general, any situation where the data flow is not continuous, `reset_physics_interpolation()` will need to be called to prevent streaking. In some limited situations, this is done for you, but it should be your first port of call.

This is mentioned in the docs:
https://docs.godotengine.org/en/3.6/tutorials/physics/interpolation/physics_interpolation_quick_start_guide.html
(I'm not sure about 4.x docs, as I'm not maintaining 4.x, indeed there are several particle features which aren't yet implemented in 4.x.)

Some details are not gone into, because it is subject to change where the auto-resets will happen.

We've added some _minimal_ auto-resets, from memory this occurs when first adding to the tree (there may be more), but most other circumstances you are expected to call reset.

Auto-resets is more complex than you would think to implement without regressions:
* Godot nodes have complex logic for deferring transform updates, and resetting stale transforms would cause glitches
* Different nodes have different order of operations and require special cases and regression testing
* Auto-resets have complex logic and extra maintenance burden (although obviously if they save a lot of user work they are worth it)
* Once we add an auto-reset, it is difficult to remove in terms of backward compatibility
* In some cases auto-resets can _interfere_ or _prevent_ the ability to achieve smooth motion where "priming" is required

For these reasons we've been very conservative adding auto-resets so far, are seeing where the pain points are, and will add them for these cases were possible.

_As an aside, there is actually an auto-reset when calling set_physics_interpolation_mode(). But it currently only occurs on going from interpolated to non-interpolated. I'm investigating whether this was to cure a glitch that way around, or it is simply a historical bug(!) and I maybe intended it to auto-reset here (it is 3 years old lol 😀 )._
I've added a fix PR above which should be easily portable to 4.x (for the non-hidden issues).

The idea is generally that you would build your scenes in the editor and set their interpolation modes etc (physics interpolation is always off in the editor).
> 
> So getting that to be seamless at runtime is more of a feature request, and would need a use case, but it can probably be done simply with a reset on the root node as you are doing.

Here's my use case: I want physics interpolation enabled globally when the refresh rate differs from the physics rate, and disabled otherwise. I have all my logic run at 60 FPS for those running less powerful monitors so that they can still get a smooth experience (that, and 60 FPS is the classic rate used for many retro games). For high refresh rate monitors, I want to enable physics interpolation, as 2D scrolling feels *very* clean at 240hz and I want to take advantage of this where possible. I also want to allow users to change this themselves based on preference (or if they need to force it off because they need to see the action frame by frame for speedrunning or analysis purposes).

The fact that physics interpolation can be adjusted globally at runtime, yet causes significant issues if used this way, says to me that both this and #101195 are bugs, not enhancements.

> * Godot nodes have complex logic for deferring transform updates, and resetting stale transforms would cause glitches

I only want to reset the previous transform, not the current one. The problem is that the previous transform isn't being set when it should be.

> * Auto-resets have complex logic and extra maintenance burden (although obviously if they save a lot of user work they are worth it)

The fix I currently have in my local code actually removes some of this code to simplify the logic.

> * Once we add an auto-reset, it is difficult to remove in terms of backward compatibility

In Godot 4's case, physics interpolation was only added for 4.3 (and only for 2D), so breaking backward compatibility would be less severe here. Also personally I think it's worth breaking compatibility if it fixes core issues with no good workaround (reverse Z-buffer, pixel snapping fixes), as long as users are made aware of potential breakage.

> * In some cases auto-resets can _interfere_ or _prevent_ the ability to achieve smooth motion where "priming" is required

The lack of auto-reset, on the other hand, means you can't easily avoid ghosting when priming in certain scenarios.

> I've added a fix PR above which should be easily portable to 4.x (for the non-hidden issues).

This PR doesn't fix the issue as illustrated in the second MRP, because it doesn't reset invisible nodes (those will still shake violently once they're made visible again).

> Here's my use case: I want physics interpolation enabled globally when the refresh rate differs from the physics rate, and disabled otherwise. I have all my logic run at 60 FPS for those running less powerful monitors so that they can still get a smooth experience (that, and 60 FPS is the classic rate used for many retro games). For high refresh rate monitors, I want to enable physics interpolation, as 2D scrolling feels _very_ clean at 240hz and I want to take advantage of this where possible. I also want to allow users to change this themselves based on preference (or if they need to force it off because they need to see the action frame by frame for speedrunning or analysis purposes).

That's a valid but quite niche use case. Instead of changing the engine architecture to enable such use case, I would suggest using the features already available to change project settings based on user configuration:

- Detect, or let users select, their refresh rate (and if relevant, whether they want physics interpolation) in your game's settings
- Save that config as an `override.cfg` that will be applied on top of the default `project.godot`
- Tell user to restart the game to take new settings into account

Sure, being able to refresh such things on the fly without a restart is _neat_, but it's not critical and most games, even AAA, often require users to restart to adjust settings which have a drastic impact on rendering.

> The fact that physics interpolation can be adjusted globally at runtime, yet causes significant issues if used this way, says to me that both this and [#101195](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/101195) are bugs, not enhancements.

I'd argue then the bug is that we allow to toggle physics interpolation at runtime. At the minimum this should be flagged as an advanced, unsupported use case that requires manual resets. But otherwise we can unexpose it altogether.

> That's a valid but quite niche use case. Instead of changing the engine architecture to enable such use case, I would suggest using the features already available to change project settings based on user configuration:
> 
> * Detect, or let users select, their refresh rate (and if relevant, whether they want physics interpolation) in your game's settings
> * Save that config as an `override.cfg` that will be applied on top of the default `project.godot`
> * Tell user to restart the game to take new settings into account

This doesn't take multiple monitors into account (my current setup is a 240hz monitor and a 60hz monitor).

> > The fact that physics interpolation can be adjusted globally at runtime, yet causes significant issues if used this way, says to me that both this and [#101195](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/101195) are bugs, not enhancements.
> 
> I'd argue then the bug is that we allow to toggle physics interpolation at runtime. At the minimum this should be flagged as an advanced, unsupported use case that requires manual resets. But otherwise we can unexpose it altogether.

I am already using this in multiple shipped games. If you unexpose it now it will cause breakage.
